embezzle

/em-BEZ-uhl/ - rhymes with pretzel · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Embezzle means to steal money entrusted to one's care by falsifying records.

The mill's payroll clerk embezzled for years by keeping a retired welder on the books and pocketing each ghost paycheck.

Worked Example

The hotel's night manager embezzled quietly for a decade: he voided one room charge each evening, took the cash himself, and initialed the register so the shortfall never showed.

Embezzle is narrower than steal. A burglar takes what was never his to touch; an embezzler is the trusted insider — the clerk, the manager, the keeper of the accounts — who is handed the money legitimately and then quietly rewrites the records to keep it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

misappropriate: Misappropriate is the broad legal term for putting entrusted money or property to your own use, and it covers careless misuse as well as outright theft. Embezzle is its narrower, harsher cousin: the trusted insider not only takes the funds but falsifies the records to hide the taking.

siphon: Siphon means to drain money off little by little through a hidden channel — the picture is a slow, quiet leak. Embezzle can involve siphoning, but it adds the legal core: the money was entrusted to your care, and the books are doctored to cover the loss.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

safeguard: to protect the funds placed in your care

reimburse: to pay money back to where it belongs

Where it sits · how elaborately the theft is engineered — pilfer → skim → embezzle

pilfer vs. embezzle: Pilfer is petty and opportunistic — pens from the supply closet; it stops far short of embezzle's engineered scheme.

skim vs. embezzle: Skim comes closer — quietly shaving cash off the day's take — but it still stops short of embezzle, which rewrites the books themselves to bury a larger theft.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — em-

Prefix — em-: in, on - here an intensifier: thoroughly

Root — bezzle

Root — bezzle: to make off with; to destroy - Anglo-French besiller, origin unknown

Put it together

Put it together: Em- + besiller = to thoroughly make away with. The em- is this unit's genuine prefix in its before-b spelling, but its partner is a mystery guest: Anglo-French besiller meant 'to plunder, to destroy,' and nobody knows where it came from before that. English courts adopted embezzle early and sharpened it to one precise crime: stealing what was entrusted to you.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Besiller left no other offspring in English — embezzle is the family's sole survivor. The prefix is real, but there is no root to reuse, so learn the word whole and let the em- remind you that the thief is on the inside.

Strength Check

Word Choice

legal / journalistic

Embezzle is the precise word when a trusted insider steals funds and doctors the records; courts, auditors, and reporters all reach for it. If the money was grabbed rather than entrusted, it is theft or robbery, not embezzlement — and misappropriate covers sloppier misuse of entrusted property that stops short of outright stealing.
